summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applicants. The policy is challenged in federal courts, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; trans and nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad.

Same-sex marriage remains formally contested in the territory. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it. In 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory whose attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. In January 2016 a district court judge confirmed by the Senate told legislators he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date; the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar, then the United States Department of the Interior. As of mid-2024 the local ban was still treated on-island as operative, with its constitutional durability an open question under academic study.

Trans-specific violence and protection machinery are documented. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case against the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local cultural context shapes daily expectations. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, frames fa'afafine as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture; reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and homosexuality is widely accepted within Samoan culture compared with neighbouring Pacific states.
tangentialFactors:
American Samoa's 2015 position was exceptional within the United States territories: its attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still being reviewed, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. No licence application had been made at that point.

Samoan cultural norms place behavioural expectations on everyone regardless of orientation. Reserved public conduct is expected across the board, so public affection or gender-nonconforming presentation may draw comment for reasons of custom rather than statute, even where homosexuality is widely accepted in comparison with neighbouring Pacific states such as Fiji.

Practical guidance for trans and nonbinary travelers under the current federal document rules is published by Lambda Legal, which sets out which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records and the current status of document updates, and by the Human Rights Campaign, whose 2025 travel and passport guidance covers the sex-assigned-at-birth requirement for new and renewed passports.
localsOnly:
Territorial employers have faced federal consequences for anti-trans conduct: the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case against the American Samoa Government in September 2023 over harassment of a transgender employee, and a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the territorial government over her gender identity.

The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 through the merger of the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, and re-anchors fa'afafine to cultural pride. Fa'afafine are defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, described as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, within a wider narrative of colonial suppression and contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Marriage recognition remains unused in practice. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa records that no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence in the territory, and sets out a litigation route beginning in the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar and continuing to the United States Department of the Interior. In July 2024 Samoa News reported an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether the territory's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment alongside questions on collectivistic and individualistic orientation.

The territory's own legislative history on marriage is on record. The Fono Senate rejected a ban bill in March 2003 introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it; at that hearing the fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source any American Samoa statute or administrative procedure for changing gender markers on territorial documents such as local identification or driver's licences; the marker rules established here are federal passport rules. Whether the territorial government issues any local document reflecting a changed gender marker is unresolved on this record.

The effect of EO 14168 and EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding within American Samoa is not sourced at the service level. The orders and their funding reach are documented; concrete reductions in available care on-island are not, and this remains unresolved.

No American Samoa provision on hate-crime enhancement for anti-trans violence, and no local penalty schedule for the conduct described in the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge, appear in the inventory. The charge itself is documented; its outcome is not.

The ACLU's challenge to the federal document policy was pending as of the source material, so the current passport posture rests on a policy under active federal litigation with no final ruling recorded here. Whether any court will restore the X marker or other non-binary markers is unresolved.
